Worked example 2 — ∂μVμ\partial_{\mu}V^{\mu}∂μ​Vμ is a scalar, and what that does to charge conservation

Show that ∂νVμ\partial_{\nu}V^{\mu}∂ν​Vμ is a (1,1)(1,1)(1,1) tensor and hence that ∂μVμ\partial_{\mu}V^{\mu}∂μ​Vμ is a scalar. Then read Chapter 0.7's continuity equation in that light.

Step 1. Differentiate the vector law. Using the covector law (2.4.11) for ∂ν′\partial'_{\nu}∂ν′​ and then the vector law for V′μV'^{\mu}V′μ:

∂ν′V′μ  =  (Λ−1)βν ∂β(ΛμαVα). \partial'_{\nu}V'^{\mu} \;=\; (\Lambda^{-1})^{\beta}{}_{\nu}\,\partial_{\beta}\Big(\Lambda^{\mu}{}_{\alpha}V^{\alpha}\Big). ∂ν′​V′μ=(Λ−1)βν​∂β​(Λμα​Vα).

Now use the fact recorded under (2.4.9): for a Lorentz transformation every entry of Λ\LambdaΛ is a constant, so ∂β\partial_{\beta}∂β​ passes straight through it:

∂ν′V′μ  =  Λμα (Λ−1)βν  ∂βVα, \partial'_{\nu}V'^{\mu} \;=\; \Lambda^{\mu}{}_{\alpha}\,(\Lambda^{-1})^{\beta}{}_{\nu}\;\partial_{\beta}V^{\alpha}, ∂ν′​V′μ=Λμα​(Λ−1)βν​∂β​Vα,

which is exactly the (1,1)(1,1)(1,1) transformation law. So ∂νVμ\partial_{\nu}V^{\mu}∂ν​Vμ is a tensor: sixteen numbers that transform correctly.

Step 2. Contract μ\muμ with ν\nuν. By §5.1's theorem, contracting a (1,1)(1,1)(1,1) gives a (0,0)(0,0)(0,0) — a scalar. So

∂μVμis the same number in every inertial frame. \partial_{\mu}V^{\mu} \quad\text{is the same number in every inertial frame.} ∂μ​Vμis the same number in every inertial frame.

The four-divergence is an invariant. Note what is not claimed: ∂0V0\partial_{0}V^{0}∂0​V0 alone is not invariant, and neither is ∂iVi\partial_{i}V^{i}∂i​Vi. Only the sum, with the index correctly paired, is.

Step 3 — cashing it. Chapter 0.7 §6 derived the continuity equation ∂ρ∂t+∇⋅J=0\pdv{\rho}{t}+\nabla\cdot\vv J=0∂t∂ρ​+∇⋅J=0 from nothing but "stuff is neither created nor destroyed", and noted at the end that ρ\rhoρ and J\vv JJ assemble into Jμ=(ρc,J)J^{\mu}=(\rho c,\vv J)Jμ=(ρc,J). Take that seriously and expand ∂μJμ\partial_{\mu}J^{\mu}∂μ​Jμ, remembering x0=ctx^{0}=ctx0=ct so ∂0=∂∂x0=1c∂∂t\partial_{0}=\pdv{}{x^{0}}=\tfrac1c\pdv{}{t}∂0​=∂x0∂​=c1​∂t∂​:

∂μJμ=∂0J0+∂iJi=1c∂∂t(ρc)+∇⋅J=∂ρ∂t+∇⋅J. \partial_{\mu}J^{\mu} = \partial_{0}J^{0} + \partial_{i}J^{i} = \frac1c\pdv{}{t}\big(\rho c\big) + \nabla\cdot\vv J = \pdv{\rho}{t} + \nabla\cdot\vv J. ∂μ​Jμ=∂0​J0+∂i​Ji=c1​∂t∂​(ρc)+∇⋅J=∂t∂ρ​+∇⋅J.

The factors of ccc cancel exactly, which is the arithmetic reason JμJ^{\mu}Jμ is defined with the ccc in the time slot. So

  ∂μJμ=0   \boxed{\;\partial_{\mu}J^{\mu} = 0\;} ∂μ​Jμ=0​

is the same equation as Chapter 0.7's continuity equation. Not an analogue: the same equation, rewritten.

But it now says more than it did. In Chapter 0.7 it was an equation about a particular observer's ρ\rhoρ and J\vv JJ, in a particular frame, with a time derivative singled out. Here the left side is a scalar and the right side is zero — a scalar equation — so by §6 it holds in every frame with the same form. If charge is conserved for one observer it is conserved for all of them, and the two-term split into "rate of change here" and "flow away from here" is just how each observer happens to slice a single four-dimensional statement. Chapter 0.7 could not have told you that; it did not have the machinery. The whole content of the upgrade is the index placement.

Grind box — where Step 1 breaks, and why Part III needs a new derivative

Step 1 above used one thing beyond the definitions: that Λμα\Lambda^{\mu}{}_{\alpha}Λμα​ is constant, so ∂β\partial_{\beta}∂β​ passes through it. Suppose it is not — as it is not for a change to polar coordinates, or an accelerating frame, or any coordinate patch on a curved manifold. Then the product rule gives an extra term:

∂ν′V′μ  =  (Λ−1)βν[Λμα ∂βVα  +  (∂βΛμα)Vα⏟inhomogeneous]. \partial'_{\nu}V'^{\mu} \;=\; (\Lambda^{-1})^{\beta}{}_{\nu}\Big[\Lambda^{\mu}{}_{\alpha}\,\partial_{\beta}V^{\alpha} \;+\; \underbrace{\big(\partial_{\beta}\Lambda^{\mu}{}_{\alpha}\big)V^{\alpha}}_{\text{inhomogeneous}}\Big]. ∂ν′​V′μ=(Λ−1)βν​[Λμα​∂β​Vα+inhomogeneous(∂β​Λμα​)Vα​​].

The first term is the tensor law. The second is not proportional to ∂V\partial V∂V at all — it is proportional to VVV itself — so the whole expression is not of the form (matrix)×\times×(components of ∂V\partial V∂V). ∂νVμ\partial_{\nu}V^{\mu}∂ν​Vμ is not a tensor under general coordinate changes.

Look closely at why this is fatal rather than annoying. The failure is an inhomogeneous term, and §6's theorem needed the transformation law to be homogeneous. With an inhomogeneous term, an expression that vanishes in one frame need not vanish in another — the proof of the central theorem collapses, and with it the guarantee that makes tensor equations worth writing.

The repair is to invent a new derivative ∇μ\nabla_{\mu}∇μ​ which differs from ∂μ\partial_{\mu}∂μ​ by a correction term chosen so that the two inhomogeneous pieces cancel. The correction is called the connection, it is built from derivatives of the metric, and constructing it is Chapter 3.3. Its failure to commute with itself is curvature, which is Chapter 3.4, which is gravity.

So: the flat-space simplification that let this chapter be short is exactly the thing Part III gives up, and everything hard about general relativity is downstream of one product rule.

10 · Your turn

Problem 1 — δ\deltaδ versus η\etaη

(a) Show that δμν\delta^{\mu}{}_{\nu}δμν​ — defined to be 111 when μ=ν\mu=\nuμ=ν and 000 otherwise, in every coordinate system — really is a (1,1)(1,1)(1,1) tensor, for any invertible coordinate change, not just Lorentz ones. Note that this is the same style of definition that failed disastrously for NμN^{\mu}Nμ in (2.4.1); explain why it succeeds here.

(b) ημν\eta_{\mu\nu}ημν​ also has the same components in every inertial frame. Show this is a special property of Lorentz transformations and not a general one, by exhibiting a coordinate change under which the components of η\etaη change.

Solution

(a) Apply the (1,1)(1,1)(1,1) law to the array δ\deltaδ and see what comes out:

Λμα (Λ−1)βν  δαβ  =  Λμα (Λ−1)αν  =  δμν, \Lambda^{\mu}{}_{\alpha}\,(\Lambda^{-1})^{\beta}{}_{\nu}\;\delta^{\alpha}{}_{\beta} \;=\; \Lambda^{\mu}{}_{\alpha}\,(\Lambda^{-1})^{\alpha}{}_{\nu} \;=\; \delta^{\mu}{}_{\nu}, Λμα​(Λ−1)βν​δαβ​=Λμα​(Λ−1)αν​=δμν​,

using (2.4.12) in the last step. The transformation law maps the array δ\deltaδ to itself, so declaring it to be δ\deltaδ in every frame is consistent with the tensor law. And no step used any property of Λ\LambdaΛ beyond invertibility, so this holds for every smooth coordinate change whatsoever.

Why this succeeds where (2.4.1) failed. The two definitions have the same form — "these components, in every frame" — but only one of them is compatible with the transformation law. Declaring components in all frames is not automatically wrong; it is an extra condition, and it is legitimate exactly when the transformation law happens to reproduce those components. For δ\deltaδ it does. For (1,0,0,0)(1,0,0,0)(1,0,0,0) it does not: boosting it gives (γ,−γβ,0,0)≠(1,0,0,0)(\gamma,-\gamma\beta,0,0)\neq(1,0,0,0)(γ,−γβ,0,0)=(1,0,0,0). The test is mechanical, and you should run it whenever you are tempted to fix components in all frames.

(b) By the same test: (2.4.16), ημνΛμρΛνσ=ηρσ\eta_{\mu\nu}\Lambda^{\mu}{}_{\rho}\Lambda^{\nu}{}_{\sigma}=\eta_{\rho\sigma}ημν​Λμρ​Λνσ​=ηρσ​, says exactly that the (0,2)(0,2)(0,2) law maps η\etaη to itself. But that identity is the definition of a Lorentz transformation. It is not available for other coordinate changes.

Counterexample: rescale one spatial axis, x′1=2x1x'^{1}=2x^{1}x′1=2x1, everything else unchanged. Then Λ11=2\Lambda^{1}{}_{1}=2Λ11​=2 and (Λ−1)11=12(\Lambda^{-1})^{1}{}_{1}=\tfrac12(Λ−1)11​=21​, so

η11′=(Λ−1)α1(Λ−1)β1 ηαβ=(12)2η11=−14  ≠  −1. \eta'_{11} = (\Lambda^{-1})^{\alpha}{}_{1}(\Lambda^{-1})^{\beta}{}_{1}\,\eta_{\alpha\beta} = \Big(\tfrac12\Big)^{2}\eta_{11} = -\tfrac14 \;\neq\; -1. η11′​=(Λ−1)α1​(Λ−1)β1​ηαβ​=(21​)2η11​=−41​=−1.

The components changed, as they must — measuring xxx in half-metres has to show up somewhere, and it shows up in the metric. A second, more consequential example: switch the spatial part to plane polar coordinates, x=rcos⁡θx=r\cos\thetax=rcosθ, y=rsin⁡θy=r\sin\thetay=rsinθ. Chapter 0.6 §4's grind box computed dx2+dy2=dr2+r2dθ2\dd x^{2}+\dd y^{2}=\dd r^{2}+r^{2}\dd\theta^{2}dx2+dy2=dr2+r2dθ2, so

ημν′=diag(1, −1, −r2, −1) \eta'_{\mu\nu} = \mathrm{diag}\big(1,\,-1,\,-r^{2},\,-1\big) ημν′​=diag(1,−1,−r2,−1)

in coordinates (ct,r,θ,z)(ct,r,\theta,z)(ct,r,θ,z) — position-dependent, in flat spacetime, with no gravity anywhere. That is the punchline worth carrying into Part III: a position-dependent metric does not by itself mean curvature. Telling the two apart requires an object that is zero for the polar metric and nonzero for a genuinely curved one, and constructing it is Chapter 3.4.

A′0=54(3−35⋅1)=54⋅125=3,A′1=54(1−35⋅3)=54⋅(−45)=−1,B′0=54(2−35⋅1)=54⋅75=74,B′1=54(1−35⋅2)=54⋅(−15)=−14, \begin{aligned} A'^{0} &= \tfrac54\big(3-\tfrac35\cdot1\big) = \tfrac54\cdot\tfrac{12}{5} = 3, & A'^{1} &= \tfrac54\big(1-\tfrac35\cdot3\big) = \tfrac54\cdot\big(-\tfrac45\big) = -1,\\[3pt] B'^{0} &= \tfrac54\big(2-\tfrac35\cdot1\big) = \tfrac54\cdot\tfrac75 = \tfrac74, & B'^{1} &= \tfrac54\big(1-\tfrac35\cdot2\big) = \tfrac54\cdot\big(-\tfrac15\big) = -\tfrac14, \end{aligned} A′0B′0​=45​(3−53​⋅1)=45​⋅512​=3,=45​(2−53​⋅1)=45​⋅57​=47​,​A′1B′1​=45​(1−53​⋅3)=45​⋅(−54​)=−1,=45​(1−53​⋅2)=45​⋅(−51​)=−41​,​

with A′2=2A'^{2}=2A′2=2, A′3=0A'^{3}=0A′3=0, B′2=0B'^{2}=0B′2=0, B′3=1B'^{3}=1B′3=1 unchanged. So A′μ=(3,−1,2,0)A'^{\mu}=(3,-1,2,0)A′μ=(3,−1,2,0) and B′μ=(74,−14,0,1)B'^{\mu}=\big(\tfrac74,-\tfrac14,0,1\big)B′μ=(47​,−41​,0,1). Contract:

A′⋅B′=(3)(74)−(−1)(−14)−(2)(0)−(0)(1)=214−14=5.  ✓ A'\cdot B' = (3)\big(\tfrac74\big) - (-1)\big(-\tfrac14\big) - (2)(0) - (0)(1) = \tfrac{21}{4}-\tfrac14 = 5. \;\checkmark A′⋅B′=(3)(47​)−(−1)(−41​)−(2)(0)−(0)(1)=421​−41​=5.✓

The naive sum. In SSS: 6+1+0+0=76+1+0+0=76+1+0+0=7. In S′S'S′: 214+14+0+0=224=5.5\tfrac{21}{4}+\tfrac14+0+0=\tfrac{22}{4}=5.5421​+41​+0+0=422​=5.5. Different. The naive sum is not a scalar, it is not the "length" of anything, and the fact that it is what you would compute in Euclidean space is exactly why the metric has to be written explicitly.

A useful habit: notice that A′μA'^{\mu}A′μ and B′μB'^{\mu}B′μ are individually quite different from AμA^{\mu}Aμ and BμB^{\mu}Bμ — A1A^{1}A1 even changed sign — while the contraction did not budge. That is the shape of every calculation in relativity worth doing.

Problem 3 — symmetric against antisymmetric

Let Sμν=SνμS^{\mu\nu}=S^{\nu\mu}Sμν=Sνμ and Aμν=−AνμA_{\mu\nu}=-A_{\nu\mu}Aμν​=−Aνμ​. Prove that SμνAμν=0S^{\mu\nu}A_{\mu\nu}=0SμνAμν​=0 identically — no conditions, no special frames. Then say where you expect this to be used.

Solution

Call the sum X≡SμνAμνX\equiv S^{\mu\nu}A_{\mu\nu}X≡SμνAμν​. Both indices are dummies, so rename them, swapping the letters: X=SνμAνμX = S^{\nu\mu}A_{\nu\mu}X=SνμAνμ​. That is not a manipulation of the object, only of the notation — the same 256256256 terms in a different order. Now use the two hypotheses on the renamed expression: Sνμ=SμνS^{\nu\mu}=S^{\mu\nu}Sνμ=Sμν and Aνμ=−AμνA_{\nu\mu}=-A_{\mu\nu}Aνμ​=−Aμν​, so

X  =  SνμAνμ  =  Sμν(−Aμν)  =  −X. X \;=\; S^{\nu\mu}A_{\nu\mu} \;=\; S^{\mu\nu}\big(-A_{\mu\nu}\big) \;=\; -X. X=SνμAνμ​=Sμν(−Aμν​)=−X.

Hence 2X=02X=02X=0 and X=0X=0X=0. ■\blacksquare■ Note that the proof is pure index bookkeeping: no metric, no frame, no dimension. It holds in any number of dimensions and for any pair of contracted slots.

Where it gets used. Constantly, and usually to make an unwanted term disappear.

  • Chapter 2.6: FμνF^{\mu\nu}Fμν is antisymmetric, so contracting it with anything symmetric kills the term. In particular ∂μ∂νFμν=0\partial_{\mu}\partial_{\nu}F^{\mu\nu}=0∂μ​∂ν​Fμν=0, because ∂μ∂ν\partial_{\mu}\partial_{\nu}∂μ​∂ν​ is symmetric in μν\mu\nuμν by Clairaut's theorem (Chapter 0.6 §6). Applying ∂ν\partial_{\nu}∂ν​ to ∂μFμν=μ0Jν\partial_{\mu}F^{\mu\nu}=\mu_{0}J^{\nu}∂μ​Fμν=μ0​Jν then forces ∂νJν=0\partial_{\nu}J^{\nu}=0∂ν​Jν=0: Maxwell's equations require charge conservation, they do not merely permit it. That is this one-line lemma doing real work.
  • Chapter 3.3: the connection is symmetric in its lower indices, so contracting it with an antisymmetric object drops out — which is why the exterior derivative of Chapter 3.5 needs no connection at all.
  • Chapter 3.6: the Einstein tensor is symmetric, so only the symmetric part of any candidate source can appear — which is a constraint on what the right-hand side of the field equations is allowed to be.

Problem 4 — counting

In nnn dimensions, count the independent components of a symmetric rank-2 tensor and of an antisymmetric one, and verify the two counts sum to n2n^{2}n2. Specialise to n=4n=4n=4 and identify what each of the two numbers will turn out to be. Then do n=3n=3n=3 and explain the historical accident that makes the magnetic field look like a vector.

Solution

Symmetric. Tμν=TνμT^{\mu\nu}=T^{\nu\mu}Tμν=Tνμ, so the array is determined by the entries with μ≤ν\mu\le\nuμ≤ν. There are nnn diagonal entries and 12n(n−1)\tfrac12 n(n-1)21​n(n−1) strictly-upper ones (half of the n2−nn^{2}-nn2−n off-diagonal entries), giving

n+n(n−1)2=2n+n2−n2=n(n+1)2. n + \frac{n(n-1)}{2} = \frac{2n+n^{2}-n}{2} = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}. n+2n(n−1)​=22n+n2−n​=2n(n+1)​.

Antisymmetric. Aμν=−AνμA^{\mu\nu}=-A^{\nu\mu}Aμν=−Aνμ forces Aμμ=−AμμA^{\mu\mu}=-A^{\mu\mu}Aμμ=−Aμμ for each fixed μ\muμ (no sum), hence Aμμ=0A^{\mu\mu}=0Aμμ=0: the diagonal is empty. Only the strictly-upper triangle survives: 12n(n−1)\tfrac12 n(n-1)21​n(n−1).

Sum. 12n(n+1)+12n(n−1)=12n[(n+1)+(n−1)]=n2\tfrac12 n(n+1)+\tfrac12 n(n-1)=\tfrac12 n\big[(n+1)+(n-1)\big]=n^{2}21​n(n+1)+21​n(n−1)=21​n[(n+1)+(n−1)]=n2. ✓ — as required, since (2.4.27) writes every rank-2 array as symmetric plus antisymmetric, uniquely, so the two pieces must account for all n2n^{2}n2 numbers exactly once.

n=4n=4n=4. Symmetric: 12⋅4⋅5=10\tfrac12\cdot4\cdot5=\mathbf{10}21​⋅4⋅5=10. Antisymmetric: 12⋅4⋅3=6\tfrac12\cdot4\cdot3=\mathbf{6}21​⋅4⋅3=6. And 10+6=16=4210+6=16=4^{2}10+6=16=42. ✓

The ten is the metric gμνg_{\mu\nu}gμν​ of Chapter 3.3 — the gravitational field is ten functions, which is why general relativity is ten coupled equations and not one. (Four of the ten are pure coordinate freedom, leaving six genuine ones; that count is Chapter 3.6's business.) The six is the electromagnetic field tensor FμνF^{\mu\nu}Fμν of Chapter 2.6: three components of E\vv EE and three of B\vv BB, and now you know in advance that there is exactly enough room and not one slot to spare.

n=3n=3n=3. Symmetric: 666. Antisymmetric: 333. The antisymmetric count coincides with the number of components of a vector — solve 12n(n−1)=n\tfrac12 n(n-1)=n21​n(n−1)=n and you get n=3n=3n=3 (or the trivial n=0n=0n=0), so this happens in three dimensions and nowhere else. That coincidence is why the curl of a vector field can be packaged as a vector (Chapter 0.7 §4.4) and why B\vv BB is written as one.

The disguise is detectable, though. An antisymmetric object dressed as a vector reveals itself under reflection: reflect space and a true vector flips its components, while these — built from a determinant-like construction, hence carrying an extra factor of det⁡Λ=−1\det\Lambda=-1detΛ=−1 as in (2.4.32) — do not. Hence "axial vector", "pseudovector", and the right-hand rule, which is a convention we are forced to state because we have insisted on describing a six-slot object with three-slot notation. In four dimensions the problem simply does not arise, because there 6≠46\neq46=4 and nobody is tempted.

The brick you just laid

You now have the definition the rest of the book runs on. A tensor of type (p,q)(p,q)(p,q) is an object whose components transform with ppp Jacobians and qqq inverse Jacobians — not a matrix, not an array, not a picture. Upper and lower indices are two different species: vectors transform like dxμ\dd x^{\mu}dxμ, covectors like ∂μf\partial_{\mu}f∂μ​f, and they pair to give a number that every observer agrees on because the two Jacobians collapse to a δ\deltaδ. You saw that measured, not asserted, in the figure: components moving in opposite directions while their contraction sat at 3.500000003.500000003.50000000 and the arrow went on piercing exactly three lines.

You have the metric as the dictionary between the species — Vμ=ημνVνV_{\mu}=\eta_{\mu\nu}V^{\nu}Vμ​=ημν​Vν, which flips three signs and is a linear map rather than a typographical convenience — and you know that η\etaη having fixed components is a defining property of Lorentz transformations, not a law of nature. You have the three operations that stay inside the class, with contraction proved. And you have the theorem the chapter exists for: a tensor equation true in one frame is true in all of them, because the transformation law is linear and homogeneous and therefore maps zero to zero. That is why every fundamental law from here on will be written with matched indices, and why F=ma\vv F=m\vv aF=ma cannot be.

Where this gets spent. Immediately, in Chapter 2.5, which writes dynamics as dpμ/dτ=fμ\dd p^{\mu}/\dd\tau=f^{\mu}dpμ/dτ=fμ and gets E=γmc2E=\gamma mc^{2}E=γmc2 out of a contraction. Then Chapter 2.6, where §7's count of six becomes FμνF^{\mu\nu}Fμν and E\vv EE and B\vv BB stop being two fields. Then Part III, where the definition is reused verbatim with one change — Λ\LambdaΛ acquires position dependence — and that single change costs you the ordinary derivative (Chapter 3.3's connection), buys you curvature (Chapter 3.4), and produces Gμν=8πG Tμν/c4G_{\mu\nu}=8\pi G\,T_{\mu\nu}/c^{4}Gμν​=8πGTμν​/c4 (Chapter 3.6), which is a tensor equation and could not have been anything else. Chapter 5.2 writes field theory in this language because it must, and Chapter 6.4 writes Yang–Mills in it because the gauge field is a connection in the same sense as Chapter 3.3's.

Chapter 2.5 now takes the definition and does physics with it.
